name: farkle-r5
context:
ROUND 5. You returned REVISE naming the Solved Game trap as the strongest remaining reason the game would be unsatisfying. I built the instrument to test it and the result inverts the objection.

─────────── YOUR OBJECTION, QUOTED ───────────

'By tuning the multiplier so precisely that the optimal depth is a narrow, predictable band, you risk turning the push from a moment of visceral tension into a moment of sterile calculation. If the player feels they are merely executing a mathematically optimal script to avoid a penalty, the juice will feel like a thin veneer over a cold, deterministic engine.'

─────────── MY FIRST TEST OF IT WAS VACUOUS ───────────

I measured the per-hand optimal stop depth over 3000 hands and got a wide spread — d1 11%, d2 24%, d3 29%, d4 21%, d5 10%, d6 5%, entropy 2.38 bits of a possible 2.58 — and almost reported that as proof the game is not solved.

It proves nothing. The distribution came out IDENTICAL for flat, x1.35 and x1.5, which is the tell. Hindsight-optimal depth is always 'as deep as this hand happened to survive', because both the run total and the multiplier increase monotonically with depth. I was measuring how deep hands go, not where judgement lives. Recorded because it is the second vacuous measurement this project has caught in its own work, and the pattern — a statistic that cannot vary with the thing it is supposed to be testing — is the one to watch for.

─────────── THE CORRECT TEST, AND IT ANSWERS YOU ───────────

The question is not whether the optimum moves. It is whether a RULE THE PLAYER CAN READ OFF THE SCREEN captures the available value. Three tiers on identical hands, 4000 seeds:

  SCRIPT    best fixed stop-depth, using no information at all
  READABLE  best fixed threshold on the risk signal the interface ALREADY SHOWS
  CEILING   hindsight optimum, which knows the future and is unattainable

  curve   SCRIPT        READABLE            CEILING   HEADROOM
  flat    2058 (d2)     2360 (risk>=3)      2501       6.0%
  x1.35   2778 (d2)     4872 (risk>=3)      6844      40.5%
  x1.5    3412 (d3)     6549 (risk>=3)     10177      55.4%

HEADROOM is what is left above a rule printed on the screen.

THE SOLVED GAME YOU DESCRIBED IS THE CURRENT DESIGN, NOT THE PROPOSED ONE. At flat reward a player following 'bank when the risk reads CRITICAL' lands within SIX PERCENT of hindsight-perfect play. There is almost nothing above the rule, which is exactly the sterile calculation you named — and it is what ships today.

The multiplier does not create that trap. It escapes it. At x1.35 the readable rule leaves 40.5% on the table, so knowing when to break the rule is worth more than the rule.

One more number from the same run: READABLE beats SCRIPT by 75% at x1.35 (4872 against 2778). The risk instrument earns its place on the screen — a player who reads it does far better than one who counts chains — while still leaving most of the value to judgement.

─────────── YOUR OTHER FINDING, ACCEPTED ───────────

You named 42-46 (HD polish) as the likely cargo cult: 'not derived from the Monte Carlo harness or the game's mathematical core. They are markers of professional execution rather than gameplay-driven necessities.' Accepted without argument. They are reclassified as EXECUTION QUALITY rather than design, they make no gameplay claim, and only 46 keeps a hard gate because a dropped frame during a chain trace corrupts the one input the game has.

I am also keeping your answer to (b) as the design rationale rather than mine: when EV is tied the decision moves to variance, so 'a player trailing in a tournament will choose the higher-variance path while a leader will choose the lower-variance one.' That is a better statement of why the tie is the point than anything in my brief, and it makes the multiplier a MODE-DEPENDENT decision — which is the argument for why VS and SOLO feel different without needing different rules.

─────────── WHAT CHANGES IN THE FIFTY ───────────

1 is now justified by headroom rather than by the depth tie: x1.35 because it lifts headroom above a readable rule from 6.0% to 40.5%. 2 is superseded — the tie was the weaker argument. ADDED 51: HEADROOM ABOVE THE READABLE RULE IS A SHIPPING GATE, measured every build, and a design change that drops it under 25% fails. ADDED 52: the risk instrument must stay worth reading — READABLE over SCRIPT is reported alongside it, currently +75%. 42-46 are reclassified as execution quality, no gameplay claim.

─────────── STILL UNMEASURED ───────────

Every audio and haptic item. The coop pair-ranking. HUMAN-CAL remains an uncalibrated stub reported as one. And the headroom figure is computed against MY risk signal — a better instrument would shrink it, which means the gate is a floor on judgement, not a proof of it.

questions.text: Headroom above a readable rule is 6.0% at flat reward and 40.5% at x1.35. Does that measurement actually rebut the Solved Game objection, or is 'a rule on the visible signal' too weak a benchmark to stand in for a competent player?

My first test of your objection was vacuous and I caught it because the answer was identical across three multipliers. Is there a similar invariance in the headroom test that would make IT vacuous too?
The headroom gate is computed against the risk signal I designed. A better instrument shrinks headroom. Does that make the gate self-serving, and if so what would replace it?
Is x1.35 the right choice, or does 55.4% headroom at x1.5 make the steeper curve the better design despite moving the optimum to depth 3?
Is this design now ready to build, or name the one thing that must be settled first.
